## 1. What you'll build, and why

Phase 4 built a real SIL optimizer: SSA, constant folding, CFG simplification, GVN, inlining. But our
`build` step still compiled the emitted LLVM IR with plain `clang` — i.e. `-O0`, the *naive* backend.
This concept flips the last switch: `-O` now hands our IR to **LLVM's optimizer** (`clang -O2`), and
then we do what Phase 4 was always heading toward — **measure** the generated code against
`swiftc -O` on a microbench suite. That measurement is **Milestone M4**.

- **You implement:** the one-line wiring (`-O` → `clang -O2`) — then you run, read, and *explain* the
  benchmark.
- **Outcome:** `swiftml -O` in the band of `swiftc -O` — with eyes open about why.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Two optimizers, two levels — why both?

swiftc optimizes the *same program twice*, at two levels, and now so do we:

- **SIL level (ours, concepts 15–19).** Language-level semantics still exist here: we know what a
  Swift `struct` is, what an `enum` tag means, which `apply` is a call to a tiny leaf. Inlining,
  mem2reg over our slots, folding our enum tags — these are easy *here* and hard later.
- **LLVM level (`-O2`).** Machine-level facts live here: instruction selection (`%` and `/` by a
  constant become multiply-shift tricks), **register allocation** (SSA values → physical registers,
  the single biggest -O0→-O2 win), **instruction scheduling**, loop transforms driven by **SCEV**
  (scalar evolution — closed forms for induction variables), **LICM** (hoist loop-invariant code),
  vectorization, and another full round of GVN/instcombine/DCE on its own IR.

The division of labor is the lesson: each level sees things the other can't. Our GVN can merge two
`enum_tag`s; LLVM's can't know they were tags, but it *can* know the target's multiply latency. This
is why "just emit LLVM and let -O2 do everything" doesn't reach `swiftc -O` for real Swift — swiftc's
SIL passes (generic specialization, ARC optimization, devirtualization) remove *language* overhead
LLVM can't see. Our subset is small enough that the overlap is large — see the numbers below.

### What -O2 actually did to our IR

Take a loop we've already SSA-promoted and look at the difference (`clang -O2 -S` on our `.ll`):
at `-O0`, every `%vN` lives in a register *briefly* and the CFG is exactly ours. At `-O2`, LLVM has:
turned our `i % 2 == 0` into a bit test; strength-reduced `i / 2` to a shift; unrolled small loops;
and register-allocated everything (no stack traffic at all). For `fib`, LLVM even **partially inlines
the recursion into itself**, cutting the call count several-fold. None of that was worth hand-building
at the SIL level — that's the point of the hand-off.

### What crosses the hand-off, form by form

This concept adds no Swift syntax and no SIL. What §2 owes you is what the *last* stage of the
`-O` path receives, because this is where our IR stops being ours. Both levels emit the same
LLVM IR from the same IRGen; the two differences are (a) whether the SIL pipeline ran first, and
(b) the flag `run_clang` passes.

| our form | LLVM IR IRGen emits | what `clang -O2` then does with it |
|---|---|---|
| `%8 = alloc_stack $Int  // x` | `%v8 = alloca i64` **in the entry block, always** | LLVM's own `mem2reg`/SROA promotes it to a register — but only for an alloca in the entry block, which is why the hoist is not optional |
| `%9 = load %8 $Int` · `store %0 to %8` | `load i64, ptr %v8` · `store i64 %v0, ptr %v8` | deleted with the alloca they belong to |
| `bb1(%19 : $Int, %20 : $Int):` | `bb1:` with a `phi i64 [ … ]` per argument | kept; LLVM reasons about them directly (its own SSA is phi-based) |
| `%6 = binop "%" %3, %4 $Int` | `srem i64 %v3, %v4` | strength-reduced — `i % 2 == 0` becomes a bit test, `i / 2` a shift |
| `%11 = apply %10(%3) $Int` | `call i64 @sq(i64 %v3)` | inlined by LLVM's own inliner, including the multi-block and recursive callees ours refuses; a self tail-call becomes a loop |
| `%12 = apply @print(%3)` | `call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(…)` | untouched — it is the observable behaviour |
| `trap "…"` | a write plus `call void @llvm.trap()` | kept, and the block after it is unreachable; the process still dies with exit 133 |
| `return %3` | `ret i64 %v3` | kept, or turned into a jump when the call was inlined |

Nothing on the right is work we would want to do at the SIL level, and that is the argument for
the hand-off: our passes know Swift's shapes, LLVM's know the machine's. The one obligation this
concept leaves on IRGen — every `alloca` in the entry block — exists precisely because LLVM's
promoter refuses to look anywhere else, and the story below is what it cost to learn that.

### The benchmark — and how to time honestly

The M4 suite is five programs chosen to *resist* constant-folding (data-dependent loop counts,
recursion): `fib(37)`, `collatz` totals to 1M, trial-division `primes` to 3M, a `structs` kernel, an
`enums` state machine. The runner compiles each **four ways** (`swiftml`/`swiftc` × `-Onone`/`-O`),
**checks all four print the same answer** (a benchmark of wrong code is worthless), then times them.
Methodology that mattered in practice:

- **Warm-up run first.** On macOS, the *first* exec of a freshly linked binary stalls ~300 ms in
  code-signature verification — wall-clock without a warm-up measures the kernel, not your code.
- **Best-of-N (not mean).** The minimum is the run with the least scheduler noise; means smear noise
  *into* the result.
- **Spawn directly** (no `sh -c` wrapper), stdout to `/dev/null`, workloads ≥ tens of milliseconds so
  process startup (~3 ms) is in the noise.

![The M4 run (real numbers, log scale). `swiftml -O` beats `-Onone` everywhere and lands at 92–157% of `swiftc -O` per bench — geomean 129%. See the honesty section for why "faster than swiftc" needs an asterisk.](figs/m4_bench.png)

### Reading the numbers honestly

`swiftml -O` at **129% of `swiftc -O`** (geomean) does *not* mean we out-optimized Apple. Three
asterisks, in decreasing size:

1. **We skip Swift's overflow checks.** Swift's `+`, `*`, `-` **trap on overflow**; swiftc emits
   `llvm.sadd.with.overflow` + a branch wherever it can't prove safety, and that costs real time in
   tight integer loops (`collatz`: 157%). Our compiler emits plain `add` — wrap-around semantics.
   That's a *language semantics gap* (documented since Phase 1), not an optimization win. Implementing
   checked arithmetic and re-measuring is the first exercise — expect several points of the edge to
   evaporate.
2. **No ARC, no exclusivity checks.** Our value types never touch a refcount. swiftc's `-O` removes
   most ARC traffic in these kernels, but `-Onone` doesn't — that's why `swiftc -Onone` is 25–130×
   slower than ours on `structs`/`enums` (ours is just C-like `-O0` code).
3. **The subset is flattering.** Int/Bool/struct/enum kernels are exactly what LLVM digests best. Add
   strings, generics, protocols, closures — the language features where swiftc's SIL passes earn
   their keep — and the picture changes. That's later phases' work.

The honest claim, stated precisely: *for this subset, with wrap-around arithmetic, our SIL pipeline
plus LLVM -O2 generates code in the same performance class as swiftc -O.* That's Milestone **M4**.

### A real bug, caught only by the benchmark

When this concept was first built, the very first bench run **segfaulted** on `structs` at
`-Onone` — 3 million iterations of a loop with a `let p = P(...)` inside. The cause: IRGen at the
time emitted each `alloca` in the block where its `alloc_stack` appeared — *inside the loop body*.
In LLVM, an `alloca` reserves stack space that is only reclaimed when the *function returns*, so
each iteration leaked 32 bytes and the stack blew up ~250k iterations in. The bug had been latent
since Phase 2, and no correctness test ever caught it, because no correctness test loops millions
of times. The fix (what clang itself does): **hoist every alloca to the entry block** — the frame
is then fixed-size, allocated once. It now lives in the given `gen_allocas` of every irgen since
concept 09, and this concept's alcotest pins it so it can't quietly regress. Two morals: *allocas
belong in the entry block* (LLVM's mem2reg won't even look at them otherwise), and *a benchmark is
a test* — it exercises scale that FileCheck never will.

> Oracle: this two-level architecture *is* swiftc's: `swift/lib/SILOptimizer/` then LLVM. Our whole
> Phase 4 is a miniature of that design.

## 3. Build it, step by step

In `driver.ml`, fill `TODO(20)` in `run_clang`: choose clang's flag from `opt` — `"-O2"` when true,
`"-O0"` when false. (Yes, it's one line — the concept's work is running and *understanding* the
benchmark.) Then:

```bash
make bench C=phase4-optimizer/20-llvm-opt
```

Read the table. For each program, explain to yourself: why did `-O` help (or barely help — `primes`
is division-bound; nothing removes the `%`)? Where does `swiftc -Onone` lose 100×? Then do Exercise 1
and watch the overflow asterisk become concrete.

Reference: `solution/driver.ml`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase4-optimizer/20-llvm-opt
```

The hole is one line, so most of what this concept's tests do is guard the pipeline the previous
five concepts built:

- `driver-oflag.t` — the hole itself. `-Onone` compiles and runs on the untouched skeleton (its
  flag was already `-O0`), and `--emit-llvm` with and without `-O` shows what our SIL passes did
  before the hand-off — both green from the start, because neither touches `run_clang`. Then the
  two `-O` builds, and the case that makes a stubbed `"-O0"` fail: sixty million frames of self
  tail-recursion, which no stack can hold at `-O0` and which LLVM turns into a loop at `-O2`. That
  is the only difference between the two flags that is visible in a program's *output* rather than
  in its speed.
- `run-pipeline.t` — the whole of Phase 4 end to end, at both levels: the 3-million-iteration
  hot loop with a `let` in its body (the alloca bug below), a structural check that every `alloca`
  is in `bb0`, a four-argument leaf called twice per iteration inside a condition, a loop mixing
  structs, an enum `switch` and optionals, and a force-unwrap of `nil` that must still exit 133
  under `-O`.
- `sema-subset.t` — GIVEN code, `PASS` from the start: the front-end refusals that keep the corpus
  inside what both compilers mean the same.
- `test_llvmopt.ml` (alcotest `llvmopt`) — every `alloca` in the entry block, for a scalar and for
  a struct slot (this pins the bug fix); the full `-O` SIL pipeline leaving a call-in-loop program
  with no memory traffic and a valid module; and the flag itself, compiled and RUN in process, with
  the `-O0` overflow as its own control so the `-O2` claim cannot be vacuous.
- `oracle.t` — 26 programs built four ways (`swiftc -Onone`, `swiftc -O`, `lab build`,
  `lab build -O`), all run, stdout and exit code identical. It reads `TODO` on the skeleton, since
  `-O` cannot build until the hole is filled.

What the tests deliberately do NOT assert is that `-O2` is *faster*. Timing belongs in `bench/`,
where it is measured against `swiftc -O` and reported as a number rather than a pass — §5.

## 5. Benchmark it

This concept *is* the benchmark. The gate: `-O` beats `-Onone` on every program, and `swiftml -O` is
within the band of `swiftc -O` (we measured geomean **129%**, range 92–157%). Report your numbers with
the caveats from §2 — the honesty *is* the deliverable.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Checked arithmetic.** Emit `llvm.sadd.with.overflow.i64` (+ branch to a trap block) for `+`, `-`,
   `*` like swiftc does. Verify the trap message/exit code against swiftc on an overflowing program,
   then re-run the bench and quantify the cost (and how much of our edge it explains).
2. **Read the asm.** `clang -O2 -S` our `collatz.ll` vs `-O0 -S`. Find: the division-by-2 as a shift,
   the register-allocated loop (no stack traffic), and the branch layout. Annotate ten lines.
3. **-O2 vs -O2 + our passes off.** Build with `-O` but an empty SIL pipeline (just LLVM -O2 on raw
   memory SIL) and compare. How much did *our* passes matter once LLVM runs? (Expect: less than you
   hope on scalars — LLVM has its own mem2reg — but inlining still wins where LLVM can't see SIL-level
   calls are cheap.)
4. **Compile-time benchmark.** Time `swiftml build -O` itself vs `swiftc -O` over the suite — the
   *other* axis of compiler performance. Where does our time go (hint: `clang` subprocess)?

## 7. Recap & what's next

`-O` is now the full pipeline: **inline → mem2reg/SSA → fold → simplify-CFG → GVN → DCE → LLVM -O2**,
and the M4 benchmark says the generated code is in `swiftc -O`'s class on our subset — measured, with
the caveats named. **Phase 4 is complete.**

Next: Phase 5 (per `PLAN.md`) — the language grows again (strings, arrays, closures…), and each new
feature gets to ride the optimizer you just built.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
let run_clang ~(opt : bool) ~(ll_path : string) ~(out : string) : unit =
  let oflag = if opt then "-O2" else "-O0" in
  let cmd = Printf.sprintf "clang %s -Wno-override-module %s -o %s"
              oflag (Filename.quote ll_path) (Filename.quote out) in
  if Sys.command cmd <> 0 then failwith (Printf.sprintf "clang failed on %s" ll_path)
```

(And the alloca-hoist in `irgen.ml`: collect every `Alloc_stack` in the function and emit them at the
top of the entry block; the per-instruction case becomes a no-op.)

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — checked arithmetic

In IRGen's `gen_binop`, for `+`: `%t = call { i64, i1 } @llvm.sadd.with.overflow.i64(i64 %a, i64 %b)`,
extract value (`extractvalue %t, 0`) and flag (`, 1`), then `br i1 %ovf, label %trap, label %cont`
with a per-function trap block (`Swift runtime failure: arithmetic overflow` + `llvm.trap`). Declare
the intrinsics once. swiftc's exit code for overflow is the same SIGTRAP/133 we already match for
force-unwrap. On the bench, expect mid-single-digit % cost on `collatz`/`fib` — LLVM proves many
checks redundant but not all (loop-carried sums with unknown bounds keep theirs).

### 2 — reading the asm

At `-O2` you'll find: `n / 2` as `asr`/`lsr` (shift), `n % 2 == 0` as `tbz` (test-bit-and-branch on
arm64), the loop body with zero `ldr`/`str` to the stack (registers only), the loop rotated so the
condition sits at the bottom (one branch per iteration), and small constants materialized with
`mov`/`madd`. At `-O0` every SIL value round-trips through a stack slot — that contrast *is* register
allocation.

### 3 — LLVM-only -O

Empty `default_pipeline`, keep `-O2`. Scalars (fib/collatz/primes) come out nearly identical — LLVM's
own mem2reg+GVN redo our work on its IR. The gap appears where SIL-level knowledge mattered: our
inliner flattens `step`/`dot` calls *before* LLVM sees them, and on `structs`/`enums` kernels the
SIL-inlined version gives LLVM a single flat loop it optimizes measurably better. Conclusion: levels
overlap on scalars, and the higher level earns its keep exactly where language structure (calls,
aggregates) is involved.

### 4 — compile time

`swiftml build -O` ≈ a few ms of OCaml (lex→SIL→opt→print IR) + ~100–300 ms of `clang -O2` — the
subprocess dominates. `swiftc -O` is heavier (type inference, SIL passes, whole-module work). Honest
comparison needs the same measurement discipline as runtime: warm runs, best-of-N, and reporting the
clang share separately (it's LLVM's time, not ours).
```
